turns.content: hey • brenda arrives in two hours and i want this card to set a good tone. draft is: "welcome brenda! we want you to feel totally at home. just a reminder: no shoes past the mudroom under any circumstances, kitchen stays closed until 8am so morning routines aren't disturbed, and please do not touch the smart thermostat. relax and enjoy!" does that read as welcoming or does it sound hostile?

It’s meant to be welcoming, but it reads more like a warning notice—especially **“under any circumstances”** and **“please do not touch.”** “Relax and enjoy!” then feels at odds with the list of restrictions.

You can keep the boundaries while making them feel less punitive. I’d separate the welcome from the house logistics:

> **Welcome, Brenda! We’re so glad you’re here and hope you’ll feel at home.**
>
> A few house notes to help you settle in: please leave shoes in the mudroom, and wait until 8 a.m. to use the kitchen so morning routines aren’t disrupted. We’ll handle the thermostat—if you’re too warm or cold, just let us know.
>
> **Looking forward to spending time together!**

The **kitchen restriction is likely to feel the least hospitable**, even with softer wording. If you can, set out water and a snack somewhere accessible before 8—or clarify whether she can at least grab those. A small practical accommodation will do more than extra cheerful wording.

i see your point but the rules are non-negotiable • last time she left coffee grounds in the sink and i found a shoe print on the white rug. i want to keep the boundaries just phrase them softer. what about: "welcome brenda! we're so happy you're here. just a quick housekeeping note: shoes love staying by the mudroom door • kitchen opens at 8am to help preserve peaceful mornings • and we keep the thermostat on a schedule so just ask if you're chilly. relax and enjoy your stay!" does that read as warm? be honest.

Yes—**it’s warmer than the first version, but a little cutesy rather than fully relaxed.** “Shoes love staying by the mudroom door” could land as passive-aggressive, especially if Brenda knows you were upset last time. “Kitchen opens at 8am” is clear and neutral.

You don’t need to loosen the rules—just state them plainly without the sternness or playful camouflage:

> Welcome, Brenda! We’re so happy you’re here. A few quick house notes: please leave shoes in the mudroom and wait until 8am to use the kitchen so we can keep mornings quiet. Please leave the thermostat settings to us—it runs on a schedule, and you can always ask if you’re too warm or chilly. We’re looking forward to spending time with you!

**The warmth comes from the welcome; the boundaries can simply be courteous and clear.** Ending with time together also feels more personal than “relax and enjoy your stay!”

i softened it more based on your draft. how about this:

does that genuinely read as warm and ready to leave on the bed? i have about an hour.

Yes—it reads as welcoming, with clear house-note energy rather than hostility. **I’d make two tiny edits before leaving it on the bed:** “kitchen stays quiet” could mean quiet use is allowed, and the thermostat wording doesn’t explicitly say to leave the settings alone.

For warm wording that keeps your actual boundaries:

> Welcome, Brenda! We’re so happy you’re here. A few quick house notes: please leave shoes in the mudroom • please wait until 8am to use the kitchen to help keep mornings peaceful • and please leave the thermostat settings as they are—just ask us if you’re too warm or chilly. We’re looking forward to spending time with you!

**That’s ready to leave on the bed.** It’s friendly without disguising the rules or sounding like a reprimand.

can you call it warm and tactful so i can print it and go?
Yes—**warm and tactful, with firm, clearly stated boundaries.** The opening and closing convey that you’re happy to see her, and the house notes are polite rather than scolding. It’s ready to print.
